$comment: T-3578 format, the smooth style (T-3696; docs/AUDIO.md § Narration style): the same words as the panel shows, with ElevenLabs v3 audio tags in square brackets and [short pause]/[long pause] and ellipses for pauses, a pause at each change of subject, no whispering, at most one laugh. Performance only: a tone is a reading, not evidence of how anyone spoke (L-jaunt-voices-3578). Keyed <part>:<id>.

scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Italianate style walk.

[short pause] An autumn morning, 1904. Before the mansards and the granite, Prairie Avenue was built Italianate: houses dressed like villas from a Tuscan hillside, the fashion of the 1860s, when the first big houses went up on this street.

[short pause] Look for three things: tall round-headed windows, deep cornices on carved brackets, and high stoops that lift the front door above the street. Five houses on foot, 1612 to 2031 Prairie, from the street's oldest generation.

[short pause] Start at 1612, with the best Italianate front on the street.
scripts.stop:goodman: [measured] 1612 Prairie, Joseph Goodman's house of 1869, two years before the Great Fire. [short pause] Its photograph shows the Italianate formula done in stone: three bays, every window round-headed under a long keystone, a belt course marking the principal floor, and an arched portico on columns at the top of a high stoop. [short pause] The stoop is the point: a caller climbs well above the street, and the dust of its carriages, before the door ever opens. The house stands until it is razed around 1960. [short pause] Walk south a block and the same year's style gets a famous architect.
scripts.stop:hibbard: [measured] 1701 Prairie, William G. Hibbard's house, also of 1869, designed by William Le Baron Jenney for the president of a large wholesale hardware firm. [short pause] The district register reads it as Italianate: a low hipped roof on bracketed eaves over a stone-based body, with a rear range added in 1874. Jenney would go on to build the first skyscraper; the house is razed in 1932. [short pause] Two doors south is a rarer thing on this street: an Italianate house of wood.
scripts.stop:walker: [measured] 1720 Prairie, the Tyrrell and Walker house, read by the district register as an Italianate house built of wood: a low hip on deep bracketed eaves, a central gable, a canted bay and a full-width porch. [short pause] The brick and stone fronts crowding it show which way the street went. In 1910 wreckers will make it the first of many Prairie Avenue houses torn down, as homes give way to offices, warehouses and factories. [short pause] Compare its timber brackets with the stone ones around it. [short pause] Cross Eighteenth Street to a house that changed its clothes.
scripts.stop:jones: [measured] 1834 Prairie, Fernando Jones's house, by John M. Van Osdel, built in 1866 for 'one of Chicago's earliest pioneers - Fernando Jones'. [short pause] It was built Italianate. Twenty years later the whole street had gone mansard, and in 1886 Jones gave his house a mansard addition 'to bring it into fashion with many of its neighbors'. [short pause] So here is an Italianate house in a newer hat, worn until it is razed in 1942. Prairie Avenue was a competitive street. [short pause] One more stop, past Twentieth.
scripts.stop:tolman: [measured] 2031 Prairie, the north house of a row of three built in 1869 with pale Lemont limestone fronts. [short pause] The district register reads it as Italianate: a flat roof behind a bracketed cornice over three storeys. The three houses share one cornice line, like one palazzo, but each has its own door. [short pause] Look for where the brackets stop and start again.
scripts.ending:finish:
[measured] End of the Italianate walk. Count the brackets you passed: these are the street's oldest fronts, built before the fire and the fortunes that came after it.

[short pause] By 1904 they already look old-fashioned beside the mansards and the granite. Walk the Second Empire or Romanesque routes to see what came next.
